questions.question: Explain why black mineworkers mainly used everyday resistance and describe the forms it took.
questions.expected_answer: They could not vote, were controlled by passes, contracts, compounds, compound managers and police, and had no recognised unions, so strikers risked arrest, fines, prison and dismissal without pay. They therefore used everyday resistance: desertion before the contract ended, despite pass laws, to go home or to better work; choosing between mines using information spread through home-area networks so that mines with bad reputations struggled to recruit; go-slows; refusing to go underground after accidents; complaints to recruiters and chiefs; sabotage; and compound protests over food, ill-treatment and fines. They also built burial societies, home-area associations, churches, dance teams and music for support and dignity, some of which later became the basis of political organisation.

questions.question: Describe organised strikes on the Witwatersrand between 1907 and 1920 by different groups of workers.
questions.expected_answer: White miners, with unions and votes, struck in 1907 against changes reducing white jobs, a strike broken with poor Afrikaner strike-breakers; in 1913 a strike from New Kleinfontein spread across the Rand, and in July soldiers fired on a Johannesburg crowd, killing about 20, forcing negotiations; in January 1914 a general strike led to martial law and the deportation of nine leaders. About 9 000 black workers struck in 1913 for better wages and conditions and were forced back by armed police and soldiers, and about 70 000 struck in 1920. Chinese workers from 1904 to 1910 protested, refused work, struck over wages and fines and deserted, meeting harsh punishment. Indian workers in Natal joined Gandhi's 1913 strike. The groups rarely acted together.

questions.question: Describe the growth of Johannesburg and explain how it was divided by wealth and race.
questions.expected_answer: Founded in 1886 on Randjeslaagte, it grew from a mining camp to about 102 000 people in 1896 and about 237 000 in 1911, an increase of about 135 000 or about 9 000 a year on average. Its population included black workers from across southern Africa, Afrikaners from the countryside, immigrants from Britain, Ireland, Europe, America and Australia, Eastern European Jews, Indian and Chinese traders, and coloured and Cape Malay workers, with men outnumbering women. The wealthy lived on the northern ridges in Parktown, white workers in Fordsburg and Jeppestown, and the poor of all races in crowded areas like Brickfields and Vrededorp. Authorities set aside locations by race; after plague in 1904 the council burned the Coolie Location and moved black residents to Klipspruit, later part of Soweto. Sophiatown, from 1903, allowed black freehold until 1950s removals.
